narrative:
The model estimates a 68% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors that, taken together, signal a higher risk of departure compared to colleagues who are expected to stay.

Most influential was the number of training programs you attended over the past three years. At seven or more, this is higher than most employees who stay (only 19% of stayers reach this level). Surprisingly, the model sees this extensive training as pushing you toward leaving rather than staying. It appears the organization interprets heavy recent training as preparation for an external move.

The second strongest factor is that you have received other job offers while working here. This is relatively uncommon—only 23% of employees who stay report receiving outside opportunities—yet it strongly pulls the prediction toward leaving, as it suggests you have viable alternatives.

Your total years of professional experience ranks third. With over 11 years overall, you sit in the more experienced minority (only 15% of stayers have this much tenure). This also nudges the model toward expecting you to leave, possibly because seasoned professionals are seen as more likely to seek new challenges.

Taken together, these three elements outweigh many positive aspects of your profile, such as high emotional commitment, strong recognition, and good rewards satisfaction. The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether additional internal growth opportunities could reduce the risk of departure. You may also wish to reflect on whether your current role still aligns with your long-term ambitions.
